java.prompt: What happens when Java asks for `charAt(word.length())`?
choices: It throws a StringIndexOutOfBoundsException
It prints s
It prints 5
It fails to compile
java.explanation: `word.length()` is 5, so this asks for `word.charAt(5)`. The legal indexes stop at 4, so nothing lives at 5 and the program halts on that line with a StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. "It prints s" is the answer that pulls at you, and for a fair reason: the letter s does sit at the end of the word. Its index is 4, though, not 5, because the count opened at 0. Reach it with `word.charAt(word.length() - 1)`. The code does compile, since the compiler has no way to know what that number will be before the program runs.

python.code:
s = "  hello world  "
parts = s.strip().split()
print(len(parts), parts[-1].upper())
choices: 2 WORLD
2 world
16 WORLD
3 WORLD
python.explanation: Take it one step at a time. `.strip()` trims the spaces on both ends, leaving `"hello world"`. `.split()` then breaks that at the space and gives you the list `['hello', 'world']`, which has 2 items, so `len(parts)` is 2. `parts[-1]` is the last item, `'world'`, and `.upper()` turns it into `'WORLD'`. If you picked 16, you measured the length of the string instead of the list: `len()` counts characters in a string but items in a list.

python.prompt: What can you safely do with a Python string value?
choices: Measure it, read indexes, take slices, and build a new transformed string.
Change one character in place with an index assignment.
Use it only for print messages.
Treat the character count as the final valid index.
python.explanation: Python strings are text values you can inspect and transform. Indexes start at 0, len(text) counts characters, slices stop before the second number, and methods such as upper() return a new string instead of changing the original.

java.prompt: What is the safest way to think about Java String values?
choices: A String is an object; use methods for length, indexing, transforming, and comparing text.
A String is a number that Java converts whenever needed.
Use == whenever two pieces of text should match.
String methods change the original text in place.
java.explanation: Java String values are objects with methods such as length(), charAt(), substring(), trim(), and toUpperCase(). Strings are immutable, so methods return new values. For text equality, use equals() or equalsIgnoreCase(), not ==.

javascript.prompt: What should you remember about JavaScript string methods?
choices: They read or return new text; the original string is not changed in place.
They always convert text into numbers before returning.
They make indexes start at 1.
They remove the need to check empty strings.
javascript.explanation: JavaScript strings are immutable. A method such as trim() or toUpperCase() returns a new string, so you must store or use that return value. Indexes start at 0, and length is a count, not the final valid index.

cpp.prompt: What should you remember when working with std::string?
choices: Use size(), zero-based indexes, comparisons, and concatenation while staying inside valid bounds.
Use size() as the index of the last character.
Assume indexing an empty string is safe.
Include no headers because string is built into every file.
cpp.explanation: std::string stores text, size() counts characters, and indexing starts at 0. The last valid index of a nonempty string is size() - 1. Include the string header when needed, and check emptiness before reading the last character.

python.prompt: What happens when you run `s[0] = "b"` on a string `s = "cat"`?
choices: A TypeError — strings do not support item assignment
s becomes "bat"
It silently does nothing
An IndexError
python.explanation: Strings are immutable, so assigning into one raises a TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment. Reading `s[0]` works, which is the trap. To change a character, build a new string, as in `"b" + s[1:]`, which gives "bat".

java.prompt: What does this print, given `answer` was built as `"ye" + "s"`?
choices: no match — == compares object identity, not characters
match — == compares the text
It throws a NullPointerException
It fails to compile
java.explanation: A string built at run time is a new object, so `==` (which asks whether two references point at the same object) is false, and this prints "no match". To compare characters use `.equals()`. The code compiles and runs; it just answers the wrong question.

choices: back() on an empty string is undefined behavior
back() is slower than indexing
empty() is the only way to get a string's length
back() returns the first character, not the last
cpp.explanation: Calling `back()` (or reading `text[text.size() - 1]`) on an empty string reads out of bounds, which is undefined behavior. The `empty()` check makes sure there is a last character before you ask for it. `back()` returns the final character, and the guard is about safety, not speed.

python.title: Strings concept check 1
python.prompt: What happens when Python code tries to join text and a number with `+`?
choices: It raises a TypeError. Convert the number with str(...) or use an f-string before joining it with text.
It prints Score: 10 because Python converts numbers during + automatically.
It prints only Score: and quietly ignores the number.
It raises IndexError because 10 is treated as a string position.
python.explanation: Python uses + for string joining only when both sides are strings. "Score: " + 10 mixes text and an integer, so Python raises TypeError instead of guessing. Convert the number first or write an f-string when you want text output.

java.title: Strings concept check 1
java.prompt: When does Java catch an assignment such as putting text into an int variable?
choices: Java checks types while compiling, so int n = "hello" is rejected before the program can run.
Java stores the length of the text because the variable is an int.
Java stores 0 because text cannot be converted.
Java accepts it and waits until printing to decide the type.
java.explanation: Java catches this before runtime because int and String are different types. The assignment int n = "hello" cannot compile; Java does not silently choose a number for the text.

javascript.title: Strings concept check 1
javascript.prompt: A string has length 5. Which index reads one place too far?
choices: text[text.length] reads past the end because the last character is at text.length - 1.
text[0] reads past the end because JavaScript indexes start at 1.
text[2] reads past the end because middle indexes are invalid.
text[text.length - 1] reads past the end because subtracting one is unsafe.
javascript.explanation: length is a count, not the final index. A five-character string has valid indexes 0 through 4, so text[text.length] asks for index 5. Use text.length - 1 for the final character after checking that the string is not empty.

cpp.title: Strings concept check 1
cpp.prompt: For a nonempty std::string, which index reaches the final character safely?
choices: text.size() - 1 reaches the final character; text[text.size()] steps past the valid range.
text.size() reaches the final character because size() is the count.
0 reaches the final character in every string.
text.size() + 1 is safer because it leaves room for a terminator.
cpp.explanation: std::string indexes are zero-based. If size() is 5, the valid indexes are 0 through 4. Reading text[text.size()] goes out of range, so check that the string is nonempty and use size() - 1 for the last character.

python.title: Strings concept check 2
python.prompt: Why does Python raise an index error for some string positions?
choices: Spaces never affect text comparison, so trimming is unnecessary.
`word[5]` asks for a sixth character in a five-character word.
`+` always follows numeric addition rules, even with text.
An empty string still has one blank character to index.
python.explanation: Python string indexes start at 0. A five-character word has valid positions 0 through 4, so word[5] is outside the string and raises IndexError.

java.title: Strings concept check 2
java.prompt: Why does Java throw `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` for some string positions?
choices: Spaces never affect text comparison, so trimming is unnecessary.
A five-character String has indexes 0 through 4, not index 5.
`+` always follows numeric addition rules, even with text.
An empty String still has one blank character to index.
java.explanation: Java String positions are zero-based. If a String has length 5, charAt(4) is the last character and charAt(5) is outside the valid range.

javascript.title: Strings concept check 2
javascript.prompt: Which habit helps you avoid string index mistakes in JavaScript?
choices: Skip trimming input because spaces never affect text comparison.
Count from index zero.
Use numeric addition rules for every `+` involving text.
Treat an empty string as if it has one blank character.
javascript.explanation: Start counting string positions at 0. A string with five characters ends at index 4, not index 5. This matters whenever you use bracket indexing or calculate the last valid position from length.

cpp.title: Strings concept check 2
cpp.prompt: What do you need before using std::string in a C++ file?
choices: Skip trimming input because spaces never affect text comparison.
Include the string header.
Use numeric addition rules for every `+` involving text.
Treat an empty string as if it has one blank character.
cpp.explanation: std::string lives in the standard string header. Including <string> makes the type available, and then you can use size(), indexes, comparison, and concatenation with the expected string behavior.

python.title: Strings concept check 3
python.prompt: What happens when Python code calls a string method but does not store or print the result?
choices: Assume slicing includes the stop position.
Index before checking that the string is long enough.
`name.upper()` returns uppercase text, but the program discards it.
Use indexes as if counting starts at one.
python.explanation: String methods return a value. If name.upper() is used alone, Python makes the uppercase string and immediately discards it because nothing stores, returns, or prints the result.

java.title: Strings concept check 3
java.prompt: Why can Java string comparison with `==` be misleading?
choices: Assume substring includes the stop position.
Index before checking that the String is long enough.
`==` asks whether both variables point to the same object.
Use indexes as if counting starts at one.
java.explanation: For String text equality, use equals(). The == operator checks whether two references point to the same object, which can look right in tiny examples and fail when the same text comes from input or another calculation.

javascript.title: Strings concept check 3
javascript.prompt: What should you do with the result of a JavaScript string transformation?
choices: Assume slicing includes the stop position.
Index before checking whether the string has enough characters.
Save transformed strings.
Use a character index without remembering that counting starts at zero.
javascript.explanation: String transformations return new values. If you call label.trim() or label.toUpperCase() without assigning, returning, or printing the result, the transformed text is discarded and label still holds the old string.

cpp.title: Strings concept check 3
cpp.prompt: What index habit prevents many C++ string bugs?
choices: Assume slicing includes the stop position.
Index before checking whether the string has enough characters.
Count indexes from zero.
Use a character index without remembering that counting starts at zero.
cpp.explanation: Count indexes from 0, not from 1. For std::string text = "code", c is index 0 and e is index 3. Mixing up count and index is how text[text.size()] slips into code.

python.title: Strings concept check 4
python.prompt: How do you reach the last character of a nonempty Python string?
choices: Use len(s), because the count is the last valid index.
Use s[0], because Python stores the last character first.
Assign into the last index before reading it.
Use len(s) - 1, or use the shortcut s[-1].
python.explanation: len(s) is the number of characters, so the final zero-based index is one less than that count. Python also supports negative indexes, where s[-1] means the last character.

java.title: Strings concept check 4
java.prompt: Why is a Java String method call by itself often a bug?
choices: Call a method and ignore its returned String.
Change capitalization on one side of a comparison only.
Assume every language uses the same text-comparison operator.
Store or use the returned String after trimming.
java.explanation: Java Strings are immutable. name.trim() creates a trimmed String, but name still points to the original text unless you store the returned value or pass it directly into the next step.

javascript.title: Strings concept check 4
javascript.prompt: When building a message with a JavaScript variable, what keeps the text readable?
choices: Call a method and ignore its returned string.
Change capitalization on one side of a comparison only.
Assume every language uses the same text-comparison operator.
Use template interpolation.
javascript.explanation: Template literals make inserted values clear: `Hello, ${name}` shows where the expression goes and avoids long chains of plus signs. It does not change the original string; it builds a new one.

cpp.title: Strings concept check 4
cpp.prompt: What is the difference between a string's count and its final index?
choices: Call a method and ignore its returned string.
Change capitalization on one side of a comparison only.
Assume every language uses the same text-comparison operator.
Distinguish count from final index.
cpp.explanation: size() returns how many characters exist. The final valid index is one less than that count because indexes begin at 0. Keep those two ideas separate before indexing into a string.

python.title: Strings concept check 5
python.prompt: In a Python slice such as word[1:4], where does the slice stop?
choices: It stops before the second number, so word[1:4] uses indexes 1, 2, and 3.
It includes index 4 because both ends are always included.
It starts counting at 1 only inside slices.
It changes the original string by removing the sliced part.
python.explanation: Python slices include the start position and stop before the stop position. That matches range(): word[1:4] takes indexes 1, 2, and 3. The original string is unchanged.

java.title: Strings concept check 5
java.prompt: How should Java code compare whether two String values contain the same text?
choices: Compare text with `a.equals(b)`. Reach for `==` on Strings and you are asking about memory, not about text.
Split text before checking whether the separator is present.
Store numbers as text when later code needs arithmetic.
Use the first character check when the rule depends on the whole string.
java.explanation: Use a.equals(b) when capitalization must match. The == operator asks whether two references point to the same object, which is a different question from whether their characters match.

javascript.title: Strings concept check 5
javascript.prompt: When should JavaScript code trim a string before comparing it?
choices: Trim input when appropriate.
Split text before checking whether the separator is present.
Store numbers as text when later code needs arithmetic.
Use the first character check when the rule depends on the whole string.
javascript.explanation: Trim input when extra spaces are not meaningful to the answer. For example, a typed value of " yes " should usually be trimmed before comparing it to "yes". Do not trim when spaces are part of the exact data.

cpp.title: Strings concept check 5
cpp.prompt: What should C++ code check before reading the last character of a string?
choices: Check emptiness before using the last character.
Split text before checking whether the separator is present.
Store numbers as text when later code needs arithmetic.
Use the first character check when the rule depends on the whole string.
cpp.explanation: Check that the string is not empty before using back() or size() - 1. An empty string has no last character, so reading one is out-of-bounds behavior.

python.title: Strings concept check 6
python.prompt: How can Python code compare a typed yes/no answer without being fooled by spaces or capitalization?
choices: Concatenate values before deciding whether numeric addition was intended.
Strip anything a user typed before you compare it: `answer.strip().lower() == "yes"`
Treat `null` or missing text as an ordinary string.
Ignore punctuation and spacing even when exact text matters.
python.explanation: A common safe comparison is answer.strip().lower() == "yes". strip() removes extra outer spaces, lower() normalizes capitalization, and the comparison then checks the cleaned text.

java.title: Strings concept check 6
java.prompt: How can Java compare two String values while ignoring capitalization?
choices: Concatenate values before deciding whether numeric addition was intended.
To ignore capitalization, use `a.equalsIgnoreCase(b)` instead of uppercasing both sides.
Treat `null` or missing text as an ordinary string.
Ignore punctuation and spacing even when exact text matters.
java.explanation: Use equalsIgnoreCase() when capitalization should not matter. It compares the text directly and avoids both the == reference trap and manual one-sided capitalization mistakes.

javascript.title: Strings concept check 6
javascript.prompt: What should JavaScript code remember after transforming a string?
choices: Concatenate values before deciding whether numeric addition was intended.
Read and transform text without changing the original value.
Treat `null` or missing text as an ordinary string.
Ignore punctuation and spacing even when exact text matters.
javascript.explanation: Methods such as trim(), slice(), and toUpperCase() return new text. Use that returned value; the original string variable is unchanged unless you assign the new value back.

cpp.title: Strings concept check 6
cpp.prompt: What should C++ code remember before indexing std::string?
choices: Concatenate values before deciding whether numeric addition was intended.
Create, index, compare, and combine text.
Treat `null` or missing text as an ordinary string.
Ignore punctuation and spacing even when exact text matters.
cpp.explanation: std::string supports indexing, comparison, and concatenation, but indexes must stay inside the string. size() gives the count; for a nonempty string, the last valid index is size() - 1.
